A file format for the data of a Perturb-seq screen: the counts, and what is
known about the cells and the gRNAs. It is a set of names and rules on top of
[MuData](https://mudata.readthedocs.io), an existing file format, and it is meant for any software that handles
Perturb-seq data. The
[sceptre analysis format](../sceptre-analysis-format/overview.qmd)
stores sceptre's analyses of such a file and builds on this one.

A MuData file holds one set of cells measured in several ways. Each kind of
measurement is a **modality**: a count matrix, a table with one row per cell
and a table with one row per feature. A data file has one modality for the
gRNAs, always named `grna`, and one for each other thing measured, usually
`rna`. The [example](#example) below is such a file, opened up.

The rules are in the
[specification](SPEC.md)
and the reasons for each in the
[rationale](RATIONALE.md).
A label such as D8 is a group of rules, the same in both, and D8.3 is one rule
of it.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Draft.** Anything in the format can still change. No released version of
sceptre or of pysceptre, its Python counterpart, reads or writes it yet:
adopting it in the packages and the pipeline is the next phase of the
[roadmap](https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/blob/main/ROADMAP.md).
:::

## Principles

Every choice in the format follows from these eight. Where two of them pull
apart, the earlier one wins. Open one for its reason and what follows from it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.principles("RATIONALE.md", "## The eight principles"))
```

## Choices made

The main choices beyond the principles. Each opens to its reason and, where there
was one, the alternative it was chosen over.

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The data is one MuData <code>.h5mu</code> file.</strong> <span class="where">D1</span></summary>

- **Why.** MuData is the standard of scverse, the Python single-cell ecosystem that scanpy belongs to, for one set of cells measured in several ways. Bioconductor reads and writes it too. Standard libraries open it in both languages, and one file is easy to move and publish.
- **Instead of.** A Zarr store, two `.h5ad` files, the `ondisc` format, or a folder of Parquet and matrix files. `RATIONALE.md`, D1, compares them. A Zarr variant could be added later without changing anything else.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Counts are stored by feature.</strong> <span class="where">D3</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The count matrix is cells × features, column-compressed, so one gene is one contiguous read.
- **Why.** Fitting a model goes gene by gene. With counts stored by cell, the IGVF consortium's pipeline first splits the whole file into per-gene chunk files.
- **Cost.** Files from mapping pipelines and from scanpy are usually stored by cell, and are converted once at import. The cost of converting a large file has not been measured.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Modalities are named for what was measured.</strong> <span class="where">D2</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The gRNA modality is always `grna`. Every other modality is named for its measurement (`rna`, `protein`, ...). The file marks none as the one to analyse.
- **Why.** A file can then hold a second measured modality, and any of them can be analysed later.
- **Instead of.** A name for the part a modality plays in an analysis, such as `response`.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Facts about the cell are in the shared cell table, measurements in each modality's own.</strong> <span class="where">D5</span></summary>

- **The choice.** Facts about the cell (batch, donor) are in the shared cell table. Measurements of a modality (`n_umis`) are in that modality's cell table, under their plain names. No shared column starts with a modality's name and an underscore, so software that sets the tables side by side under prefixed names (`rna_n_umis`) gets distinct names.
- **Why.** A batch belongs to the cell, not to its RNA.
- **Instead of.** Everything in one modality's cell table, or everything in the shared table.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The file's own entries are at the top level of <code>uns</code>.</strong> <span class="where">D10</span></summary>

- **The choice.** The format version (`perturb_seq_format`), the dataset's identifier (`dataset_id`) and what is known about the screen (`title`, `organism`, `genome_build`, `perturbation_type`, `source`) are scalar entries at the top level of `uns`.
- **Why.** They are facts about the dataset, so other tools should be able to read and write them. Under a key named for one tool they would belong to that tool.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>A gRNA has one target, and so do the gRNAs of one vector.</strong> <span class="where">D8</span></summary>

- **The choice.** Each gRNA has one `grna_target`. Where a vector delivers several gRNAs, they share a target. A library that combines different targets on one vector is refused.
- **Why.** What it means to combine the gRNAs of such a vector is a scientific question first. A separate table of gRNAs and targets can be added later.
- **Also.** Targets are assumed to be on the genome. A screen that targets RNA names the transcript in `grna_target` and leaves positions out.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>Target positions are 1-based, with both ends included.</strong> <span class="where">D8</span></summary>

- **The choice.** `target_start` and `target_end` count from 1 and include both ends. A file with positions gives its genome build.
- **Why.** It is the convention of GTF files, and sceptre's own example data already follow it.
- **Instead of.** Counting from 0 with the end excluded, as BED files do.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>A value some method computed stays with the analysis that uses it.</strong> <span class="where">D12</span></summary>

- **The choice.** A cell-type label, a cluster or a score is advised to be kept with the analysis, not in the data file. It is advice: a file that carries such a column still conforms. The count summaries `n_umis`, `n_nonzero` and `p_mito` are the exception the format defines.
- **Instead of.** Computed annotations in the cell table, where other formats keep them.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>The names.</strong> <span class="where">D2 to D10</span></summary>

The modality names `rna` and `grna`, and the columns `grna_target`, `target_chr`, `target_start`, `target_end`, `vector_id`, `n_umis`, `n_nonzero`, `p_mito` are sceptre's names. Other formats use other names for the same things, and none is a standard: the IGVF consortium's pipeline calls the modalities `gene` and `guide` and the target `intended_target_name`, and pertpy's example data calls them `rna` and `gdo`.

</details>

<details class="fold">
<summary><strong>What the format does not hold yet.</strong></summary>

- **gRNAs.** A target, its position, an optional vector and an optional kind. No spacer sequence, and no position of the gRNA itself.
- **Genes.** No annotation, not even gene symbols.
- **gRNA calls.** The file holds gRNA counts, so a screen delivered only as calls has no place in it.
- **Later.** The first two are optional columns that can be added without changing anything else. They are listed under [planned additions](RATIONALE.md#planned-additions-to-the-format).

</details>

## Example

The tree below is a real data file, `example/highmoi/screen.h5mu`: sceptre's
high-MOI example data, with 500 cells, 100 genes and 60 gRNAs. Open a group to
see what is in it, and an entry to see its first rows. The descriptions are
read from the specification's own files.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.screen_tree())
```

A file may have columns the format does not define, such as `response_name` in
the gene table here, which holds gene symbols. Software ignores columns it
does not know.

Two more example files are in `example/`: sceptre's low-MOI example data, and
a small made-up file that has every kind of column the format allows.

## Reading

The format has no reader of its own. A data file is read with the standard
MuData library of each language, and what comes back is a standard object held
in memory: a `MultiAssayExperiment` in R and a `MuData` in Python.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
screen <- MuData::readH5MU("example/highmoi/screen.h5mu")
screen
```

The file's own entries, and the gRNA table:

```{r}
S4Vectors::metadata(screen)[c("perturb_seq_format", "dataset_id", "genome_build")]
head(SummarizedExperiment::rowData(screen[["grna"]]), 3)
```

## Python

```{python}
import mudata

screen = mudata.read_h5mu("example/highmoi/screen.h5mu")
print(screen)
```

The file's own entries, and the gRNA table:

```{python}
print({key: screen.uns[key] for key in ("perturb_seq_format", "dataset_id", "genome_build")})
print(screen["grna"].var.head(3))
```

:::

R shows each matrix as features × cells, and Python as cells × features. It is
the same stored matrix, which each language presents in its own convention.

## Writing

The standard libraries do not write a conforming file by default: R's MuData writer, for instance, stores counts as
decimal numbers. A writer is a thin layer over the standard one that stores
counts as integers, feature by feature, and keeps to the allowed kinds of
column. `format/` has one for each language, `fmt_write_screen()` in R and
`write_screen()` in Python. They are temporary: they exist to test the format,
and the packages will write the files themselves.

## Validation

Four things check the format: a validator, a set of test files, a suite of
checks, and automatic runs of that suite on every change.

### What "conforms" means

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(f"""The specification has {counts["all"]} numbered statements of three kinds.

| Kind | What it is about | How many | How it is checked |
|---|---|---|---|
| File rule | What a file contains | {counts["file"]} | By the validator, on the file alone. The validators check {"all of them" if counts["file_checked"] == counts["file"] else str(counts["file_checked"]) + " of them"} |
| Behaviour rule | What software reading or writing a file does | {counts["behaviour"]} | By a test where one exists: {counts["behaviour_tested"]} have one |
| Guidance | Advice to whoever writes files | {counts["guidance"]} | Not checked |
""")
```

A file **conforms** when it breaks no file rule. `SPEC.md` says beside each
statement how it is checked, and which ones nothing tests yet.

### The validator

`validate_screen()` takes a file on disk and returns the rules it breaks, with
where and why. It exists twice, in R and in Python (`format/`), and both read
the same machine-readable definitions (`spec/screen.json`). Here it is on a test file in which a gRNA with a real target is
marked as a control:

```{python}
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "format")
import perturb_seq_data

problems = perturb_seq_data.validate_screen("conformance/invalid/screens/control_type_with_a_target.h5mu")
print(problems.to_string(index=False))
```

On a conforming file the result is empty.

### The conformance files

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(f"""`conformance/` holds {conforming} files that conform and {broken} files that each
break one rule or a few. `conformance/cases.json` says, for every file, which
rules a validator must report. Both validators must report exactly those, no
more and no fewer. Someone writing another validator, or a reader, tests it
against the same files.""")
```

### The suite

`verify/run.sh` runs every check, in R and in Python, and prints a summary. The
counts below are from the run this page was rendered after.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(nt.status({
    "conformance": "Both validators report exactly the expected rules on every conformance file. A few broken files, such as one with counts stored as decimal numbers, do not conform but must still be read correctly by the standard libraries, and are",
    "encodings": "Every kind of column, written by each language's standard library and read by the other's. The kinds the format allows come back correct. The kinds it forbids, such as true/false columns, do not, which is why they are forbidden",
    "independent-readers": "Tools that know nothing of this format read the example files: anndata and scanpy in Python, HDF5Array in R",
    "wide-index": "Files whose count matrices need 64-bit positions, which very large screens do. No test file is that large, so the limit is lowered for the test",
    "writers": "What a writer must do beyond producing a conforming file: a copy of a data file keeps the dataset's identifier and every modality",
}))
```

The two languages run different numbers of checks in some groups, because
each tests its own libraries.

### Automatic runs

The suite runs by itself on GitHub whenever a change is pushed to this folder,
on three fresh machines: Linux, macOS and Windows. Each installs only standard
libraries, then runs `verify/run.sh`. A failure on any of them marks the change
as failing. The current state and the history of runs are at the
[workflow's page](https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/sceptre-hub/actions/workflows/perturb-seq-data-format.yml).

### At real size

The example files are small. Once, by hand, the format was run on a real large
screen: 207,324 cells, 13,135 genes and 13,077 gRNAs. Both languages wrote the
data to identical files of 5.7 GB, both validators passed them, and both read
them back, in memory and one gene at a time from disk.

A second run used a made-up file of 2.2 billion nonzero counts, past the size
at which positions in the count matrix no longer fit in 32 bits. Python wrote,
validated and read it. R validated it and read it from disk, but cannot hold
a matrix of that size in memory, and so cannot read it whole or write it.
`scale-test/` has the numbers of both runs.
